content.comment_body: I am using a [product_name] and a [product_name] communication module, which are assigned IP addresses in the 192.168.20.x range. My regular network uses 192.168.1.x. From the 192.168.1.x network, I can access the [product_name], but not the communication module. If my PC is switched to 192.168.20.x, I am able to reach the module. Has anyone else encountered this problem?

The [product_name] uses a Class C network, meaning the IP range is 192.0.0.0 to 223.255.255.255, and the subnet mask is typically 255.255.255.0. The IP address has four parts: XXX.YYY.ZZZ.NNN. For successful communication, all devices must share the same first three IP segments; only the last segment should differ per device. For example, my PC was using 192.168.178.NNN and the [product_name] was 192.168.178.030. I tried changing the IP to 192.168.0.030 to test. The programming software indicated that the [product_name] and PC were on different subnets and suggested a temporary IP for the PC, allowing communication and program transfer. This demonstrates that the [product_name] cannot communicate directly with devices on different subnets.
If you change your PC's subnet mask to 255.255.0.0 from 255.255.255.0, it will be able to access other subnets in addition to its current subnet.
I appreciate your response. This solution is effective for me.

analysis.insight_summary: The user encountered network communication challenges between their PC and a communication module when they were on separate subnets. Other participants explained that [product_name] devices and their modules must be in the same subnet for straightforward communication, but modifying the PC's network settings can enable cross-subnet access. The provided networking guidance resolved the user's issue.
analysis.user_expectations: The user anticipates being able to communicate with both the [product_name] and its communication module from a PC located on a different IP subnet, preferably without needing to adjust the PC's networking configuration.
